results.title: Which is correct Dr. or Dr? [duplicate] - English Language &...
results.content: * related: Does the abbreviation for Saint in a church name require a period? As an Italian, I prefer **Mr** without the period, because in school we were taught that the period following an abbreviation stood for "following letters omitted", but the *r* in Mr and in Dr is the *last* letter of Mister and Doctor, so no letter following "r" is omitted. answered Feb 22, 2017 at 10:46. The rule that Henry Fowler suggests in his Modern English Usage (if memory serves; I don't have the book in front of me) is to use a period if and only if the abbreviation does not include the last letter of the full word - thus "Mr" (for MisteR) lacks a period, but "Prof." (for PROFessor) takes a period. In modern British English, usually abbreviations are written without full stop marks. answered Feb 22, 2017 at 10:07. results.title: Is Dr. the same as Doctor? Or how to distinguish these two?
results.content: # [Is Dr. the same as Doctor? [closed]](/questions/355516/is-dr-the-same-as-doctor-or-how-to-distinguish-these-two). My co-worker argued that Dr. means Doctor (as a job), while I translate it to Dr (as a title, like Master, bachelor, doctor). I think Dr is, of course, short for Doctor, which can be both a title or a job. P/S: Also, does `Dr.` as a title has anything relate to those in `{Master, Doctor, Bachelor}`? 'Dr.' is simply an abbreviation for the title 'Doctor'. Dr. should not be used to abbreviate the word 'doctor' when it is not a title, though you might find it used like that in older writings. Doctor and Dr. would be more of what you would've been thinking is Title, or Name. The example I gave for the nurse extends to other disciplines; I know people with doctorates in bioengineering and physical therapy who use the title: "Mr." It seems that it's mostly the academics that like to retain the "Dr." title.

results.content: Background is that I have to store this data in a database for both english and non-english persons, with some non-english languages requiring words from both groups to be present at the same time (as opposed to english where i.e. you would use either Dr. or Mr., but not both of them together). I'm giving this as a comment as it doesn't actually answer the question but is relevant to what you are doing.(1) You're incorrect that titles are not combined in English. The relevant Wikipedia article about English honorifics calls the former group "common titles" and the latter "academic and professional titles". > Social titles are the prefixes that go before people’s names (i.e. Mr., Mrs., Ms., Miss). Social titles are also called "courtesy titles", for example:. > Courtesy Titles: Mr., Mrs., Miss, Ms. *Courtesy title* has a specific meaning amongst the British aristocracy, and it certainly doesn't refer to ordinary things like "Mr, Mrs...".
